title: Shy From the Start
text:
Some toddlers walk into a room full of strangers and new toys and dive in. Others cling to a parent, fall silent and watch from a distance. The Harvard psychologist Jerome Kagan wanted to know whether such differences were passing moods or something deeper.

With J. Steven Reznick and Nancy Snidman, he selected toddlers who, in laboratory sessions with unfamiliar people, objects and situations, were consistently very timid, which they called behaviorally inhibited, or consistently bold and sociable, called uninhibited. The children were then seen again several times, up to about age seven.

The differences tended to persist. Many of the children who had been inhibited as toddlers were still quieter and more cautious with unfamiliar children and adults years later, while most uninhibited children stayed outgoing. The inhibited children also differed physiologically: on average they had higher and more stable heart rates and other signs of a more reactive stress system. Kagan concluded that part of shyness reflects an inborn temperament.

Yet the stability was far from complete. A good number of inhibited children became noticeably less shy over time. Kagan later suggested that parents who gently encouraged their wary children to face new situations, rather than shielding them from every discomfort, helped them change.
lesson: A shy child is not broken, and temperament is not destiny. Gentle, steady encouragement to try new things helps more than either pushing or overprotecting.
people: Jerome Kagan, J. Steven Reznick, Nancy Snidman
source: Kagan, J., Reznick, J. S., and Snidman, N. (1988). Biological bases of childhood shyness. Science, 240(4849), 167-171.
